verdicts.label: 1A
verdicts.note: A search snippet of the MDA X Plus page confirms the $2,595 price for a 25B-300 lane (3.2B read pairs per lane). When I opened the page directly I got the read table but no prices, and no user class is shown. The S4 figures ($4,933/$4,901/$5,167 member) come from FY22–24 PDFs that I could not open. The page's claim of 'up to 60% reduction' does not name the 6000 as the baseline. The comparison also crosses fiscal years. The ~2.5x gap is below the known blended 6000/X revenue-per-Gb ratio of ~3.4x, so this is a core-level datapoint and does not show the tail is less price-elastic. The finding that the core's 6000 lane price rose ~5% in FY24 is mildly new; it matches CNAG raising its 6000 price and conflicts with Salk's list cuts.

verdicts.label: 1C
verdicts.note: The press release confirms the numbers: prenatal $94.2M vs $60.9M, oncology $13.7M vs $4.9M, total $109.4M (+64%), gross margin 70% vs 65%, and FY26 guidance of $450–465M reiterated. Total tests accessioned grew only 33% (197K vs 148K), and that figure includes fast-growing oncology. The +21% ASP gain explains most of the gap between revenue growth and test growth. Prenatal test growth is not split out and is probably below 33%. Test growth of about 35% is already on the known list, so only the revenue split is new. This is weak evidence against NIPT maturation, because the Gb growth is smaller than the revenue growth suggests.

verdicts.label: 1B
verdicts.note: Vilella's Substack confirms the >450 AVITI base and $58M of 2025 revenue. GenomeWeb's ~$85M was not verified, so treat revenue as a $58–85M range from conflicting sources. The '40 units to 190' comparison in the detail is garbled and should be dropped. The 450-system base and the miss against the $100M target are not on the known list.

verdicts.label: 1C
verdicts.note: This mostly restates known items ('BillionToOne cost/test relatively stable', 'cost declines plateaued'). The Q2'26 release says cost per test 'increased slightly' on oncology mix. Cost of revenue covers much more than sequencing, so a flat cost per test does not show that sequencing deflation fails to drive volume. I folded the useful arithmetic into a derived item.

verdicts.label: 1C
verdicts.note: This is new as a named-customer filing datapoint, but it is generic 10-K risk-factor and reimbursement language. It supports the known expert view that reimbursement is the binding constraint. It does not show that volume is gated today, since the company grew tests 33%.

verdicts.label: 1B
verdicts.note: I did not verify the claim that kit shipments more than doubled; the Substack does not mention it, and the GenomeWeb summary was not read in full. The back-solved end-2024 base of ~280 (450/1.6) is arithmetic only. The utilisation inference rests on an unverified figure.

verdicts.label: 2B
verdicts.note: The Substack confirms both figures: AVITI24 at >35% of new instrument bookings, and biopharma AVITI24 bookings +175%. Counting-application pricing is described only as 'below one dollar per million reads', with no exact figure. AVITI24 is largely an in-situ multiomics instrument, and the bookings are on a small base, so this is only a weak link to research sequencing price pressure on Illumina.

verdicts.label: 1B
verdicts.note: Not verified; the Substack does not mention the clinical-research share. If revenue was $58M rather than $85M, clinical research is about $15M, not $21M. Either way it is under ~1% of Illumina's ~$1.9B clinical consumables, so this shows direction, not material pressure.

verdicts.label: 1B
verdicts.note: Duplicate of F082, which already covers the revenue miss against the $100M target. It is also mislabeled: Element's revenue speaks to competitive price pressure (1B), not Illumina's volume growth (1C). The $58M vs $85M conflict is unresolved, and the Substack, which I opened, says $58M.

verdicts.label: 1B
verdicts.note: The per-unit comparison is approximate. The initial £5.23M covers flow cells plus unsplit 'associated consumables', while the option is a cap, so the 53% lower unit price is likely overstated. The platform is not Illumina's, so the item shows only that a public buyer gets volume tiers. It is tangential to Illumina's large-account discounting.

verdicts.label: 2B
verdicts.note: Opened the page. It confirms the Ultima UG 100 is the primary WGS platform, AVITI24 is used 'where appropriate', and no Illumina platform is offered for WGS. Correction: this page lists only $221 (external, 30x on UG100). The AVITI prices come from the other UMGC page, which is already on the list as F005/F006. Only the fact that Illumina is excluded from the WGS service is incremental.

verdicts.label: 1B
verdicts.note: Restates F005, which already lists the 30x/60x/90x prices of $221/$274/$379. The ratio is simple arithmetic. The step that more depth bought on Ultima 'lowers Illumina's revenue per Gb' is not supported.

derived.label: 1C
derived.claim: At BillionToOne, a fast-growing Illumina clinical customer, all of the Q2'26 gross-margin gain came from price, and cost of goods per test rose about 4% year over year.
derived.detail: Q2'26 ASP was $551 at a 70% gross margin, which implies COGS of ~$165 per test. Q2'25 ASP was $455 at 65%, which implies ~$159 per test, so COGS per test rose about 4%. Gross profit per test rose from ~$296 to ~$386 (+30%), entirely because ASP rose 21%. Tests accessioned grew 33% while revenue grew 64%. This customer's volume and economics are being driven by reimbursement and price, not by falling sequencing costs; COGS includes far more than Illumina reagents.
derived.quote: overall cost per test rose slightly year over year
derived.why_new: The known list has only 'cost per test relatively stable'. The implied COGS per test and the split of the gain into price vs cost are new.

derived.label: 1B
derived.claim: Element's implied consumables-and-service revenue per AVITI system is at most ~$100K a year, mid-throughput scale, so near-term pressure on Illumina's high-throughput consumables is limited.
derived.detail: Element reported $58–85M of 2025 revenue (sources conflict) on a base that rose from ~280 to >450 systems, ~365 on average, with ~170 net adds. At an assumed blended instrument price of ~$290–500K, the 170 adds would bring in ~$49–85M of instrument revenue. That leaves ≤~$36M of non-instrument revenue even on the $85M figure, or ≤~$100K per average system. That compares with Illumina's guided NextSeq 1k/2k pull-through of $80–100K and NovaSeq X pull-through of ~$1.24M. The instrument price is our assumption (list was ~$289K at launch; an expert said ~$500K).
derived.source_name: Rhymes with Haystack / GenomeWeb on Element JPM 2026
derived.why_new: No implied Element pull-through or scale comparison is on the known list.

derived.label: 1B
derived.claim: At MD Anderson's core, Illumina's 10B-300 lane costs ~50% more per Gb than the 25B-300. That is about double UCLA's ~26% premium, so within-X price steps still have room to compress at cores that have not cut the 10B.
derived.detail: MD Anderson's X Plus page (search snippet, 2026) lists 10B-300 at $1,523 per lane (1.25B read pairs ≈ 375 Gb, so ~$4.06/Gb) and 25B-300 at $2,595 per lane (3.2B read pairs ≈ 960 Gb, so ~$2.70/Gb), a ratio of ~1.50x. UCLA's ratio fell from 1.58x to 1.26x after its 10B price cut (D005). If MD Anderson follows UCLA, the 10B price would fall ~16%. MD Anderson's 25B price of $2.70/Gb is in line with UCSD ($2.92) and UConn ($2.94).
derived.source_name: MD Anderson ATGC NovaSeq X Plus page
derived.quote: Up to 60% reduction in sequencing price
derived.why_new: MD Anderson's X lane prices and its 10B/25B ratio are not on the known list.
